title: InfoQ previews the September cohorts of its online certification programs
gist: InfoQ is opening September cohorts for three paid online certification programs — Architecture (Luca Mezzalira), Engineering Leadership (Michelle Brush of Google SRE), and AI-Assisted Engineering (Thoughtworks' Zichuan Xiong and Premanand Chandrasekaran) — each five weekly four-hour live sessions. The AI-Assisted Engineering track's thesis is that teams are adopting coding agents faster than they build the verification harness around them.

themes.theme: The verification gap in agentic coding

insights.claim: Teams are adopting coding agents faster than they are building the verification infrastructure around them, leaving a gap between generation capability and the ability to check output.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: The bottleneck in AI-assisted software is verification tooling, not model capability — a demand signal for CI, review-gate and test-generation vendors.
insights.quote: Teams are adopting coding agents faster than they're building the verification around them

insights.claim: The operative unit for safe agentic engineering is the 'harness' — everything outside the model, including permissions, sensors, review gates, and CI checks that let an agent correct itself before a human ever sees the change.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: 'Harness' is emerging as the naming convention for the agent-ops layer; products that map to permissions, sensors, review gates and CI checks fit an already-articulated buyer mental model.
insights.quote: The harness is everything outside the model: the permissions, the sensors, the review gates, the CI checks that let an agent correct itself before a human ever sees the change.

insights.claim: The AI-assisted engineering curriculum splits work by where the agent belongs: generation stays with the agent, while verification does not.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: A clean division-of-labor heuristic to apply when judging whether an AI-engineering product oversteps into unverifiable territory.
insights.quote: generation stays with the agent, while verification does not
insights.locator: Their cohort runs on one split throughout

insights.claim: Practical agent training now anchors on a specific commercial tool and real brownfield code: participants build a harness against a real brownfield codebase anchored on Claude Code, covering agent permissions, sensors, characterization tests, independent review, and CI for agents running unattended.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Claude Code being the default teaching substrate in professional certification is a distribution signal for Anthropic's developer-tool position.
insights.locator: Over the five weeks, participants build a harness

insights.claim: The capstone requires a write-up comparing five weeks of logged agent results against week-one predictions, plus one rule or agent skill codified from the participant's own recurring review findings.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Measuring agent output against prior predictions is a discipline most organizations skip — a cheap way to test whether claimed AI productivity gains are real.

insights.claim: Architecture training is being reframed as sociotechnical work, spending as much time on how decisions get made and defended to a CTO as on the patterns themselves, and covering decentralized decision-making, platform engineering, developer adoption, and the constraints AI agents introduce.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Architecture curricula now treat AI agents as a first-class design constraint — a leading indicator that agent governance is entering standard enterprise practice.
insights.locator: His syllabus treats architecture as sociotechnical work

insights.claim: The value proposition of cohort-based architecture education is compressing feedback loops: in practice you wait years to learn whether an architecture decision was right, and the course is designed to shortcut that.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Compressed-feedback peer learning is the differentiating claim of paid cohort education against free content — the moat if it holds.
insights.quote: In the real world, you wait years to see if your architecture was right or wrong,

insights.claim: The format is five weekly four-hour live online sessions where participants watch a conference talk beforehand and then apply a framework from it to a real decision from their own work, alongside senior engineers from other companies, with sessions deliberately not recorded to encourage open discussion.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Non-recorded, peer-cohort delivery is the format publishers are using to monetize expertise that free video cannot capture.
insights.locator: Participants watch a QCon talk before joining

insights.claim: The stated core value of these programs is the cross-company peer group working the same problems in different contexts, rather than the instructional content itself.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: If peer networks are the product, the defensibility of technical education shifts to community assembly — hard for AI-generated content to replicate.
insights.quote: The value is the peer group, working on the same problems in different contexts.

insights.claim: The engineering leadership syllabus builds toward what a system costs after it ships — capacity planning, operational load, and incident response — with earlier weeks on organizational dynamics, technical strategy and execution, and which metrics actually indicate whether a strategy is working.
insights.speaker: Artenisa Chatziou
insights.so_what: Post-ship operational cost as the culminating leadership topic reflects where engineering budget pain actually sits.
insights.locator: Her syllabus builds toward a final week
